column1: # title: HIS-201 Unit 1 — 1 Main Ideas Pathway

column2: Ice Age hunters from Asia followed megafauna across Beringia or down the Pacific coast, settling the Americas.
As megafauna died out, Mesoamericans domesticated squash, beans and maize, and stored food let the Olmecs, Maya and Aztecs build cities.
Few domestic animals meant no exposure to livestock diseases like smallpox, leaving Native Americans without immunity.

Meanwhile in Europe, the Black Death (bubonic plague, 1340s–1350s) killed a quarter of the population, giving survivors better wages and more land, while merchants' new capital financed trading ventures.
Europeans craved Chinese spices, ceramics and silks, but the Ottoman Empire controlled eastern Mediterranean trade routes, and Mehmet II's 1453 conquest of Constantinople alarmed Europe.

Seeking direct access instead, Prince Henry "the Navigator" promoted Portuguese voyages, Catholicism and opposition to Islam; caravels and the astrolabe reached West African gold, and Atlantic-island sugar plantations used West African slaves.
Believing a westward route to China was faster, Christopher Columbus sailed for Spain and in 1492 reached the Taino in the Caribbean, joining the hemispheres of cards 1 and 4.

Lacking immunity (card 3), the Aztecs fell to Hernán Cortés through smallpox, Indian allies and guns; American silver made Spain enormously rich, and the Columbian Exchange swapped crops, animals and diseases.
Martin Luther's Reformation (salvation by faith alone, the Bible as sole authority) split Europe into Catholic and Protestant states, so Protestant England saw Catholic Spain as its rival in America.
Challenging Spain, Walter Raleigh's Roanoke colony failed after Ralph Lane's men killed Wingina and the Spanish Armada delayed John White's return with supplies.
Spain held New Mexico and Florida with Franciscan missions and soldiers until forced labor and suppression of Pueblo religion sparked the 1680 Pueblo Revolt.
England's 1607 Jamestown suffered disease and gentlemen who would not farm, but Powhatan tolerated it because English trade goods and guns helped him subdue his rivals.
John Rolfe's tobacco made Virginia profitable, and the headright system (50 acres per immigrant whose passage was paid) drew indentured servants while tobacco fields took Powhatan land.

By the 1660s overproduction lowered tobacco prices, Charles II's Navigation Acts restricted trade, and freed servants moved west, so in 1676 Nathaniel Bacon led frontier farmers against Governor Berkeley.

Planter unity and the growth of Black slavery prevented new Bacon-style revolts, and after 1680 falling death rates made enslaved Africans more profitable than servants, while slave codes kept poor whites from uniting with slaves.

column1: 16. South Carolina and the Yamasee War (Ch. 3)
column2: Barbados planters carried this plantation slavery to South Carolina's rice fields, and its Indian slave trade sparked the 1715 Yamasee War.
While England planted the south, Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec (1608) on the St. Lawrence to trade for beaver with Huron allies, aided by Jesuit missionaries.
Competing for beaver, the Dutch-armed Iroquois destroyed the smallpox-weakened Hurons in the Beaver Wars, pushing France toward the Mississippi.

Unlike the Chesapeake's single indentured servants, Puritans came in family groups: Separatists signed the Mayflower Compact at Plymouth, and John Winthrop's Massachusetts Bay Colony aimed to be a "city upon a hill."

Family groups and shared Puritanism made New England stable, but it banished Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson, held the Salem witchcraft trials, and its land hunger caused Metacom's War (1675–1676).

England conquered New Netherland as New York and William Penn founded Pennsylvania for Quakers; James II then merged the northern colonies into the Dominion of New England, but the 1688 Glorious Revolution dismantled it, leaving firmly rooted colonies.
In the 1700s Spain built presidios (military garrisons) and missions in Texas and California, while French Louisiana stopped importing slaves after the 1729 Natchez uprising.

British colonies grew through natural increase (births exceeding deaths) and immigration, but Scots-Irish backcountry settlers clashed with the English coast, and enslaved Africans resisted in the 1739 Stono Rebellion.

Religion divided colonists further: the Enlightenment, championed by Benjamin Franklin, stressed human reason, while George Whitefield's Great Awakening split churches and spread Presbyterian and Baptist churches.
Despite these divisions, most white colonists were proud to be English because Britain's benign neglect gave them more land, opportunity and self-government than England had.
